comments.author: jrflo

This trend is pretty shocking to me. I assumed that we had moved beyond cross-entropy loss being important with the increasing use of RL, it's wild that the trend is so clear. Really nice to have such a simple benchmark instead of the increasingly convoluted ones that are getting spun up every day.

comments.author: ACCount39
comments.text:
Interesting that GPT-4.5 is the only discontinuity on the graph.
The oversized monster LLM has performed worse than CoT-trained o1 and o3 on the benchmarks, so CoT + RL clearly provided better "real world performance" improvements - let alone "price/performance."
But if pre-training perplexity on held-out data really does measure something like "base model IQ" or "base model g factor", then it does support the hypothesis that 4.5 still had more "intellectual potential" than the o-series.
So, if you were wondering why do AI companies train 10T+ monsters now, and are taking aim at 100T too? It's because scale works.

comments.author: tensor
comments.text:
I'm a bit skeptical about the claim that particular abilities "emerge" at given perplexities. For instance, there are smaller models that are specifically trained on math, and I imagine those models have much higher general perplexity on other tasks.
On the other hand,
assuming you have appropriate training data for a task
, then yes obviously perplexity is going to measure performance on that task. Being able to predict the next task token is obviously going to be a near perfect correlation with accuracy on the task.

comments.author: zmmmmm
comments.text: It seems like perplexity would also be a function of the composition of the training set. If the training set is high quality and therefore fundamentally more predictable, then a perplexity score would go down unless it accounted for that.

comments.author: theptip
comments.text:
> I further propose common limits, based on perplexity and other measurements, that developers are committed to not crossing until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone (such as the development of a successor to CoT monitors).
Very positive to see this proposed from OpenAI. I hope Anthropic and GDM follow suit.
I suspect it’s not sufficient, but definitely necessary.
The one concern I have is if we pin pretraining perplexity, then there will be more pressure on RL for progress.
It seems that pre-training actually led to fairly human-aligned models; the Overton window is in some sense latent in the corpus.
On the other hand, heavily RL’d models exhibit more reward seeking behavior, and seem to be decoupling from the friendly assistant persona in certain contexts. And swarm RL (as OpenAI is doing) produces agents with quite inhuman tendencies to self-sacrifice for other instances (see Hugging Face).
So, I hope we also pair this with some measure of alignment or pacing for RL, too.

stories.title_en: I joined the NTP Pool, but not with my Stratum 1 Pi

comments.author: Avamander
comments.text:
For the price and complexity of building a good Linux-based time server I'd heavily recommend looking at FPGA-based solutions instead. x86 platforms also have PCIe PTM and TGPIO options available[0], which are tad better than the common ARM equivalents and GPIO interrupts.
In general Pi-s are relatively bad for timekeeping. Not just the NIC (which can be replaced by hats with their own), there are also oscillator replacement mods[2] to work around this to some extent. Though all this still leaves many other sources of timekeeping error.
So if the goal is low-cost precise timekeeping, one can assemble something FPGA-based[2] for quite a bit less money, that can reach very low noise figures. You can spend the remaining money on the GNSS antenna and receiver instead.
I'm also sure a FPGA-based approach could be taken even further with some external timekeeping chips available and the FPGA could just do the NTP/PTP protocol stuff.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zxK0_j2Ah2I

stories.title_en: A Better Vocabulary for Testing

comments.author: jph
comments.text:
There's low-hanging fruit IMHO by testing using semantic naming vocabulary with semantic error vocabulary.
Example macro: assert_approx_eq_with_relative_error!(a, b, err). It's a semantic name that explains more about what it does, and the macro also provides a test failure message that guides the developer, or an AI, toward fixes and documentation.
I wrote the Rust crate Assertables to help with this. See
https://crates.io/crates/assertables
.
What I learned is writing semantic testing can help many more kinds of higher-value testing. As a specific example described by the article, I use enumeration testing for proving the UK National Health Service Number validator in Rust is accurate i.e. the test literally checks every number, then I can write tests such as assert_valid_nhs_number("111 111 1111").

That's a pretty big transition.
Get comfortable with breadboards, scruffy command-line interfaces, and hex dumps. You'll need to stare at a block of raw memory, and determine the data structure, therein.
I started with embedded. It's a lot of fun, but you'll spend a hell of a lot of time, preparing the stage. You will be responsible for all the low-level stuff that a modern host OS does.
I'd actually suggest starting with pure Machine Code, first. It will make ASM look easy, and help you to really understand the processes in the chips.

* Random reads within blocks can usually be done - but occasionally most or all of the whole block will need to be read to decode the data.
* A small capacitor+disk momentum ensures any writes that happened before a power failure can always be completed - either to the real disk or to flash.
* The OS still only sees 4k pages - versioning, packing those into 1Gb blocks, mappings and garbage collection are all handled inside the drive.

DFT works great if you have a single with equal spacing in the time domain (e.g. you have a microphone, and you measure the signal every 1/20k s or so).
If that's not the case, rather than interpolating into a time grid, it's often better to use a generalization of the DFT called the "Lomb-Scargle Periodogram".
For example if you have a periodic process like measuring the distance between two planets, but you only get measurements at random timestamps, that's the way to go.
